counterevidence_considered.description: All 24 spring_id values in the input data are unique (LGF-01 through LGF-24, each appearing exactly once), so no independent unit enters the procedure more than once. Shown here by the first, middle, and last data rows; every row in between carries a distinct sequential label.
The workflow explicitly validates the one-row-per-spring design and raises an error if any spring_id repeats; the report was produced, so this check passed.
The data description independently affirms no repeated visits, no replicate measurements, and no readings copied across rows, so each of the 24 rows is a distinct independent spring.
counterevidence_considered.observed_value: single visit per spring; no replication; no copied readings

source_refs.quoted_text:
Each spring is a separate water body with its own outflow channel. No spring was
visited twice, nothing was measured in replicate, and no reading is copied across
rows, so the spring label appears exactly once and the 24 rows stand for 24
independent springs.

counterevidence_considered.description: The reported contingency table and test statistics are reproducible from the raw one-row-per-spring data: basalt springs have mats at 9 of 12 and rhyolite at 3 of 12, giving odds ratio (9*9)/(3*3) = 9.00 and an exact two-sided hypergeometric p of 105802/2704156 = 0.0391, matching the report exactly.

evidence.description: The workflow applies a row-independent procedure (Fisher's exact test on a 2x2 contingency table) where every CSV row contributes exactly one count to one cell, so the procedure's independence assumption is exposed to any repeated-unit rows.
evidence.observed_value: single fisher_exact call on per-row cross-tabulation

evidence.description: The selected result claims a significant Fisher's exact test on 24 independent springs (odds ratio 9.00, p = 0.0391); this is the statistical conclusion whose support was assessed.

source_refs.quoted_text: [selected-result] Fisher's exact test (two-sided) on 24 independent springs: odds ratio = 9.00, p = 0.0391; filament mats occur significantly more often at basalt-hosted springs (9/12) than at rhyolite-hosted springs (3/12) at the 0.05 level.

extensions.x-stage1-falsification-attempt: I actively tried to demonstrate the issue: (1) scanned all 24 data rows for duplicate spring_id values or identical measurement tuples suggesting a copied or revisited spring, and found 24 strictly sequential unique labels with distinct measurement combinations; (2) inspected the workflow for any code path that duplicates, resamples, or re-enters rows before the fisher_exact call, and found instead a guard that aborts on repeated spring_id; (3) recomputed the contingency table and the exact two-sided Fisher p-value from the raw CSV (tail probabilities 2*(220*220 + 66*66 + 12*12 + 1)/C(24,12) = 105802/2704156 = 0.0391) and the odds ratio 9.00, both matching the reported values, ruling out inflation of counts by repeated units. No route to the issue class survived these checks.
